engineering_challenges.challenge: Mapping an unreliable, undocumented legacy data shape
engineering_challenges.why_hard: No schema to validate against and no ability to fix the source; correctness must be achieved defensively on the consumer side against values nobody has seen yet

engineering_challenges.challenge: Browsing a 400,000-row dataset from a browser
engineering_challenges.why_hard: Default React patterns (fetch-all-then-filter, debounce-on-keystroke) all fail at this cardinality; backend caps page size at 100

engineering_challenges.challenge: Bridging the https-to-file browser security boundary
engineering_challenges.why_hard: No technical workaround exists; the correct answer is to change the interaction model, reached after two wrong attempts

engineering_challenges.challenge: Reverse-engineering the archive's directory sharding rule
engineering_challenges.why_hard: Undocumented; only inferable from filename/location pairs; took three iterations including a revert

engineering_challenges.challenge: Inviting a user without destroying the administrator's session
engineering_challenges.why_hard: createUserWithEmailAndPassword silently replaces the session on the app instance used; invisible in the SDK's API surface

engineering_challenges.challenge: Firestore named-database access from a typed SDK
engineering_challenges.why_hard: The two-argument signature was not exposed; required a cast with a graceful fallback to the default database

engineering_challenges.challenge: Deleting 19,300 lines of plausible-looking generated code
engineering_challenges.why_hard: Required judging feature by feature what the backend could actually serve; deletion is the most judgement-heavy and least-rewarded work in a prototype-to-production transition

engineering_challenges.challenge: Choosing the right data-access architecture for the scale and shape of the problem
engineering_challenges.why_hard: The failure mode is slow and ambiguous - a managed service that nearly works absorbs a week before anyone concludes the abstraction is wrong rather than the implementation, and arguing for the boring option against a platform the team has already committed to is a social problem as much as a technical one

decisions.problem: The frontend existed on mock data; the backend did not exist
decisions.decision: Author the API contract in-repo, derived from the mock fixtures
decisions.reasoning: The prototype had already encoded the domain model; formalising it let both sides proceed in parallel
decisions.tradeoffs: Inherits the prototype's modelling mistakes; the delivered API diverged in envelope shape
decisions.result: Divergence cost nothing at runtime because the client handles both shapes

decisions.decision: One centralised integration module rather than per-component fetching
decisions.tradeoffs: 488-line file that grows with every endpoint
decisions.result: Backend shape changes absorbed in one place; UI stayed free of coercion logic

decisions.problem: Needed auth, invitation, reset and suspension quickly with no backend auth available
decisions.decision: Firebase for identity; leave the data API untouched
decisions.reasoning: Fastest path to a controllable user list
decisions.tradeoffs: The two planes are not linked, so the data API is not protected by the Firebase session; portal user state lives outside the system of record
decisions.result: Working administrable access layer delivered in one day of commits, with a security gap left open

decisions.problem: Replacing mock data would orphan every import type
decisions.decision: Keep src/data/mock*.ts as the type source of truth; stop importing the arrays
decisions.tradeoffs: Files named 'mock' that are load-bearing for types confuse newcomers
decisions.result: The data-source swap touched the API layer and pages, not the type surface

decisions.problem: Search against 400k rows measured at 4-5 seconds
decisions.decision: Separate typed query from submitted query; fire on Enter or button only
decisions.result: One expensive query per intent instead of one per keystroke

decisions.problem: Live/Not-Live counts needed without fetching rows
decisions.tradeoffs: Still a full count on the backend; two extra round-trips on load

decisions.title: Abandon Firebase Data Connect for a Node REST API over PostgreSQL
decisions.note: The most consequential decision on the project, and the one Abraham influenced rather than owned
decisions.problem: The backend developer's first approach served the dataset through Firebase Data Connect's generated GraphQL-style SDK. It was not working; roughly a week went in without a usable data path (duration REPORTED).
decisions.decision: Replace it with a conventional Node.js REST API over PostgreSQL
decisions.reasoning: The frontend needed ordinary paginated list endpoints over a very large relational dataset - what REST and SQL do natively. The generated SDK added a translation layer, an unfamiliar query model and a build-time dependency between the two developers, for nothing the application needed.
decisions.tradeoffs: Discards a week of work and the managed tooling; the team now owns an API service, its deployment and its performance characteristics
decisions.result: VERIFIED - SDK import removed and REST fetching implemented the same day, 2025-11-02; the API has served production since and was confirmed live 2026-10-10. Its pagination model is what made the limit=1 count probes and server-side paging viable.
decisions.attribution: Implemented by the backend developer. Abraham's contribution was the architectural argument (REPORTED) and the API contract it was built to (VERIFIED).

problems_solved.title: Malformed legacy timestamps broke date rendering
problems_solved.problem: Values such as 2013-01-22T00:00:00:00Z yield Invalid Date
problems_solved.solution: sanitizeDate() regex-repairs the doubled separator, re-validates, falls back to the YYYY-MM-DD prefix; paired with formatDateTime() handling a second legacy format DD-MM-YY HH:mm

problems_solved.title: Policy documents unreachable from the browser
problems_solved.problem: Filenames alone do not locate files on an undocumented sharded Windows share; browsers block https->file navigation
problems_solved.investigation: Three commits over two days; an 8-10 digit prefix rule, then a dynamic variant, then a revert to the matching rule
problems_solved.solution: Derive first-six-digits -> nn/nn/nn path with 00-prefixed filename; present in a modal with copy-to-clipboard and toast feedback

problems_solved.title: A suspended user could still authenticate
problems_solved.solution: Two-layer enforcement: Firestore query by lower-cased email (with casing retry) before the Auth call, plus a re-check in onAuthStateChanged that signs out suspended users and avoids overwriting their status when merging lastLogin

problems_solved.title: Inviting a user logged the administrator out
problems_solved.solution: Dedicated secondary Firebase app for invitations, followed by an immediate password-reset email so the invitee sets their own password

problems_solved.title: A prototype carrying ~19,300 lines of unbacked features
problems_solved.solution: Four staged cleanup commits plus an API specification defining what would actually be built

problems_solved.title: Forgot-password link submitted the sign-in form
problems_solved.problem: A Button inside a form defaults to type=submit
problems_solved.solution: type="button"; reported by a named internal user and fixed the same day

problems_solved.title: Committed secrets in .env
problems_solved.solution: Stripped values, created .env.example with key names only, added .env to .gitignore
problems_solved.qualification: Removes values from the working tree, not from Git history; rotation would be the complete fix and is not evidenced

problems_solved.title: A colleague's refactor weakened the suspension control and did not fix the bug it targeted
problems_solved.situation: On 2025-11-09 another developer made two commits aimed at sign-in button behaviour and by 11-17 had reworked AuthContext and ManageUsers. Abraham reports the refactor was produced by layering an AI tool over his authentication code.
problems_solved.problem: (1) The refactor introduced a checkedUserIds Set memoizing the Firestore status lookup, so suspended status was checked once per uid per session instead of on every auth-state change - defeating the suspension guarantee. (2) It did not fix the reported bug: commit 9cdef3f, despite its message, is a double-to-single quote reformat (35+/35-), and the forgot-password Button still had no type attribute eleven days later.
problems_solved.solution: 576ccaa restored the original auth and user-management logic across App.tsx, AuthContext.tsx, ManageUsers.tsx and SignIn.tsx (185+/228-), reinstating the unconditional status check. 39b28fc then fixed the real defect with one line (type="button").
problems_solved.result: The security control behaves as designed again; the user-facing bug was resolved the day it was escalated.
problems_solved.evidence: commits beb75a3, 9cdef3f (9 Nov), 576ccaa, 39b28fc (20 Nov); diffs inspected directly
problems_solved.evidence_level: VERIFIED (the regression and the ineffective fix) / REPORTED (that the refactor was AI-assisted)
problems_solved.why_strong: A code-review judgement call with a measurable correctness consequence, resolved by reverting rather than patching over. The one-line root-cause fix proves the large refactor was never addressing the problem.

gaps.finding: The data API served production records to an unauthenticated request; the frontend sends no Authorization header or Firebase ID token. All production figures in this dossier were obtained without credentials.
Firestore security rules are the real control for the user plane but are not in this repository and could not be reviewed

Verbose console.log of API responses remains in production code paths, which can print customer data into the browser console

The access-restriction control did not restrict access. Abraham was deliberately denied backend and database credentials as a data-protection measure while being given full frontend ownership - but the frontend is itself a fully-privileged data client. This audit read production records for 779,778 clients using nothing but the repository's own configuration and no credentials. The control reduced his ability to FIX the data layer without reducing his ability to READ the data.
gaps.classification: PRIVATE - a genuine finding, not a grievance; the professional framing is the security lesson, not a complaint about exclusion

known_code_limitations: Dashboard KPI trend percentages (8.2%, 12.4%, -2.1%) are hard-coded placeholders, not computed values
The 'Live Policies' KPI sums policiesCount across the current page of clients only
TanStack React Query is mounted but data fetching is hand-rolled useEffect + fetch, forgoing caching, retries and request de-duplication
lessons: Write the contract before the backend exists, then don't trust it - the spec unblocked parallel work and the defensive mappers absorbed the inevitable divergence; both halves were necessary
AI scaffolding produces breadth, not a product; the valuable judgement is deciding what cannot be supported
Cardinality changes which React patterns are legal - debounced live search and client-side filtering do not survive 400,000 rows
Legacy integration is mostly coercion; most of the integration layer is making a 25-year-old data model safe to render
Accept the browser's boundaries rather than fighting them
Convenience SDK calls hide stateful side effects
Under a deadline, the contract and the scope cut come first - both decisions that bought the most time happened early, when they felt like a detour from shipping

Would do differently: token-authenticate the data API from day one; integration-test the pure mapping functions; adopt the already-mounted React Query; strip debug logging; compute or remove placeholder KPI trends

A managed service that nearly works is the expensive failure mode - outright failure is cheap to diagnose, partial success is not; the signal is spending time on the tool's model of the problem instead of the problem
Influence without authority runs on artefacts, not opinions - the architectural argument landed because there was already a written API contract to point at

An access control that targets the wrong surface buys nothing - being denied database credentials while owning a fully-privileged data client restricted the ability to fix the data layer, not to read the data
Reverting is a legitimate review outcome - a refactor that turns a security check into a cache and leaves the original bug in place should be undone, not patched forward

interview_stories.theme: What you'd do differently; security maturity

interview_stories.theme: Delivering something commercially critical (pressure, prioritisation) - the strongest story here
interview_stories.situation: The company was exiting a third-party platform holding ~25 years of client and policy data. The CTO said the vendor had given about a month to extract it, with a charge over GBP 100,000 if missed, and that this was why delivery speed mattered.
interview_stories.task: Build the system that would hold and expose the extracted data so the business could use and verify what came across.
interview_stories.action: Cut scope hard before writing integration code (removed six speculative feature areas); wrote the API contract up front so extraction/backend and frontend could proceed in parallel; built the integration defensively because the incoming data was a 25-year legacy extract with no schema guarantees and there would be no second pass.
interview_stories.result: The portal shipped; the data has a home the business controls; the application has been in production use for over a year.
interview_stories.evidence: API_Specifications.md (contract-first); four cleanup commits (scope control); production data profile consistent with a bulk historical extraction. The deadline and penalty are as told by the CTO, verbally.
interview_stories.how_to_tell_it: Attribute the figure explicitly and say the deadline governed the data extraction, with the portal as the destination. Volunteering that boundary makes the story more credible, not less.

interview_stories.theme: A technical disagreement, and how you handled it (influence without authority) - the strongest seniority signal in this project
interview_stories.situation: Abraham owned the frontend; another developer owned the backend and extraction. Abraham was deliberately given no backend or database access as a data-protection measure. The developer chose Firebase Data Connect and spent about a week unable to get a workable data path out of it.
interview_stories.task: The frontend had nothing real to consume, under deadline, and Abraham had no authority over that component.
interview_stories.action: Rather than escalate it as a blocker, kept making the technical case: the application needed ordinary paginated list endpoints over a large relational dataset, which REST and SQL do natively; the generated SDK added a translation layer, an unfamiliar query model and a build-time dependency between the two developers for nothing needed. The API specification was already written, so the alternative was concrete rather than abstract.
interview_stories.result: SDK out and REST fetching in on the same day, 2025-11-02. That architecture shipped and has served production for over a year; its pagination model made server-side paging over 400,000 rows workable.
interview_stories.evidence: abandoned @irev/quote-ap dependency in package.json; listCustomers in f627567; Data Connect emulator keys disabled in .env.example above the live API base; branch data-sdk-integration; commits d4f26f5 and 750e2c8
interview_stories.how_to_tell_it: The pivot is in the repo; the role in causing it is Abraham's own account. Say both - 'I can show you the switch; you'd have to take my word that I'm the one who pushed for it.' Disarming, and it makes the rest land.

interview_stories.theme: A time you disagreed with a code change (code review, correctness over politeness)
interview_stories.situation: A colleague refactored Abraham's authentication and user-management code with AI assistance while fixing a reported sign-in bug.
interview_stories.problem: The refactor memoized the Firestore account-status lookup in a Set, so a suspended user's status was checked once per session instead of on every auth-state change - turning a security control into a cache. And it had not fixed the bug: the commit claiming to fix the sign-in button was a quote-style reformat, and the defect was still present eleven days later.
interview_stories.action: Reverted the refactor to restore the unconditional check, then traced the live symptom to its root cause - a Button inside a form defaulting to type=submit - and fixed it with one line.
interview_stories.result: The suspension control works as designed; the user-facing bug closed the day it was escalated.
interview_stories.evidence: 576ccaa (185+/228- across four files), 39b28fc, and 9cdef3f for the ineffective fix
interview_stories.why_it_lands: The one-line fix is the argument - it demonstrates the large refactor was never addressing the problem, without needing to say so.

portfolio_material.overview: A browser-based portal that opens a 25-year, 400,000-policy insurance broking archive to internal staff, built on a legacy data source with no usable schema guarantees.
portfolio_material.challenge: An AI-generated prototype with eight polished feature areas, zero real data and an invented data model; real constraints were a dataset two orders of magnitude larger than any UI pattern in it, a source returning syntactically invalid dates, and a document estate on a Windows file share browsers are forbidden to touch.
portfolio_material.my_role: Frontend/integration engineer: API contract, integration layer, authentication and user administration, prototype reduction, PR integration. A second developer owned much of the policy/risk presentation; the UI scaffold and component library were AI-generated.
portfolio_material.solution: React/TypeScript SPA on Firebase Hosting with two independent planes - Firebase Auth plus a named Firestore database for user lifecycle, and a Cloud Run REST API for broking data. All lists server-paginated; all legacy values pass through a single mapping module.
portfolio_material.results: A working, authenticated, administrable read portal over a legacy archive delivered in nine weeks, plus the specification artefact that let the backend proceed in parallel.
portfolio_material.what_id_improve: Token-authenticate the data API; test the mapping functions; adopt the already-mounted React Query; remove debug logging and placeholder KPI trends.

public_safe_claims: Built a read-only internal portal over a large legacy insurance dataset (hundreds of thousands of records, ~25 years of history) using React, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind, shadcn/ui and Firebase.
Designed a defensive integration layer that repairs malformed legacy data before it reaches the UI.
Implemented server-side pagination, submit-triggered search and lightweight count probes to make a very large dataset browsable from a SPA.
Built Firebase authentication with invitation, self-service password reset and administrable account suspension.
Reduced an AI-scaffolded prototype substantially before building the real integration, removing feature areas with no supporting data.
Solved the browser https-to-file boundary by changing the interaction model rather than attempting a workaround.
Built the destination system for a migration off a third-party platform (migration publishable in neutral terms; deadline and penalty are not)
Delivered a system that has been in production for over a year
The Data Connect to REST/PostgreSQL architecture pivot, as a technical lesson about managed data layers versus REST over SQL for large paginated datasets (employer, dataset size and timeline removed)
The revert-versus-patch-forward lesson (a memoized security check, and a one-line root-cause fix), told without reference to who wrote the refactor
private_only_information: Employer and product identifiers: Insurance Revolution, BG Insurance, 'iRev SSP Portal', nexus-renew, Firebase project bg-ssp, the Cloud Run API base URL, Firestore database name ssp-portal-users
All exact production counts (779,778 / 401,339 / 4,249 / 397,090), premium averages and the live-vs-lapsed ratio
Insurer codes, product-type codes, branch codes, scheme names, event-type taxonomy
The legacy document path convention and the Z: share layout
The observation that the data API served production records to an unauthenticated request
Internal staff names appearing in commit messages
Any customer record values observed during the audit (none are reproduced in these outputs)

The entire vendor-exit commercial story: the deadline, the GBP 100,000+ figure, the vendor's identity, and the fact that a penalty existed at all. Employer's commercial information. Excellent interview/CV material in private conversation; must not appear in a public portfolio, LinkedIn post, blog article or published CV. Even unnamed, 'a company facing a six-figure penalty from a vendor' is identifiable to anyone in the sector.

The identity of the colleague whose refactor was reverted. The engineering substance is Abraham's to tell; the person is not. Describe it as 'a colleague's refactor' and never name, hint at, or make them identifiable - including by naming the repository.

That backend/database access was withheld from Abraham, and the observation that the restriction did not actually restrict data access. Internal security posture; not publishable, and not to be raised as a grievance in interview - the lessons entry is the professional framing.

audit_methodology.attribution: git blame --line-porcelain aggregated per author, cross-checked against git shortlog commit counts; both reported because they disagree informatively
audit_methodology.production_access: HTTP GET only. No POST/PUT/PATCH/DELETE. No database connection. No credentials available or used. Raw samples written to a session scratch directory and not retained.

reproduction.policy_sampling: 4 pages x 100 live (pages 1,10,25,43 -> n=349) and 4 pages x 100 not-live (pages 1,1000,2000,3970 -> n=400)
reproduction.sub_resource_sampling: 30 live policies (random.seed(1)) and 25 historical policies (random.seed(2)); pagination.total read per policy

limitations: Sub-resource statistics are sample-based; page selection was convenience-based, not uniformly random across all 3,971 not-live pages
Latency figures are single cold measurements from one machine and network location
The backend service, legacy data store and Firestore security rules were not available for inspection
Portal usage (as opposed to data scale) could not be measured at all
git blame credits the last author to touch a line, under-crediting rewritten work and over-crediting reformatting
safety_confirmations: No credentials, keys, URLs or connection strings appear in any output file
No customer PII is reproduced in any output file

business_driver.summary: The company was exiting a third-party vendor whose platform held roughly 25 years of its client and policy data. The vendor gave approximately one month to extract the data, with a charge reported as in excess of GBP 100,000 if the deadline passed. This portal was the destination for the extracted data.
business_driver.source: Abraham, relaying what the CTO told him at project kickoff. Verbal, undocumented, not independently verifiable from this repository.
corroborated_by: Data profile is a bulk historical extraction, not an operational system: 779,778 clients, 401,339 policies of which only 1.06% are Live, events from 2000, 67 insurer codes in the historical sample
Application is entirely read-only - no POST/PUT/PATCH/DELETE against the data API anywhere in the codebase
Delivery was compressed: nine weeks end to end, with production-data integration landing in a concentrated burst on 2-3 Nov 2025
NOT_corroborated: The vendor's identity and contract terms
That this portal is what averted the charge
business_driver.important_caveat: The nine-week commit span does not evidence a sub-one-month deadline. The deadline most plausibly governed the data EXTRACTION (a separate backend workstream), with this portal as the destination. State it that way - it is more accurate and more defensible.
business_driver.how_to_phrase: The business was exiting a vendor under a contractual deadline, with a six-figure penalty if the data wasn't extracted in time - that's what the CTO described as the driver.
business_driver.classification: PRIVATE - interview and CV use with attribution only; never publish

reported_claims.claim: Built the destination system for a time-boxed third-party data exit, holding ~25 years of extracted client and policy records - reported by the CTO as avoiding a charge in excess of GBP 100,000.
reported_claims.evidence_level: REPORTED (commercial context) / VERIFIED (the system and the data it holds)
reported_claims.evidence: CTO, relayed verbally at project kickoff; corroborated in shape by the production data profile
reported_claims.qualification: Always attribute the figure. Not measured, contract terms not evidenced, and the deadline most plausibly governed the extraction workstream rather than this frontend.

reported_claims.claim: Delivered a system that has run in production for over a year without requiring further frontend changes.
reported_claims.evidence: Production API returned live data on 2026-10-10, ~11 months after the final commit
reported_claims.qualification: No commits since Nov 2025 is consistent with stability but is not proof of it; no uptime or error data.

reported_claims.claim: Provided the architectural guidance that moved the project off a failing Firebase Data Connect data layer onto the Node.js REST API over PostgreSQL that shipped and has served production since.
reported_claims.evidence_level: VERIFIED (the pivot and its date) / REPORTED (that the advocacy drove it)
reported_claims.evidence: @irev/quote-ap generated-SDK dependency and its listCustomers call (f627567); Data Connect emulator keys disabled in .env.example alongside live VITE_API_BASE; branch data-sdk-integration; SDK removed and REST implemented same day 2025-11-02 (d4f26f5, 750e2c8)
reported_claims.qualification: Abraham did NOT build the backend - another developer did, and he had no backend or database access by design. The repository evidences the pivot, not who caused it.

reported_claims.claim: Identified and reverted a refactor that had weakened an authentication control, then fixed the underlying defect in a single line.
reported_claims.evidence: 576ccaa restores the unconditional Firestore status check by removing a checkedUserIds memoization (185+/228- across four files); 39b28fc adds the missing type="button"; preceding commit 9cdef3f is a quote-style reformat that left the defect in place
reported_claims.qualification: That the refactor was AI-assisted is REPORTED; the regression and the ineffective fix are verifiable from the diffs regardless.

handling_the_scaffolding_question.situation: The repository history shows 133 commits under a scaffolding tool's bot account.
handling_the_scaffolding_question.position: That work is Abraham's - he directed the tool - and the dossier records it that way. But it is visible to anyone who opens the repo.
handling_the_scaffolding_question.recommended_answer: I prototyped the UI with a scaffolding tool, then specified the API, built the integration layer, the auth and user-admin subsystem, and cut about 19,300 lines of what the tool had produced because the data couldn't support it.
handling_the_scaffolding_question.why: More impressive than claiming to have hand-typed a shadcn component library, and cannot be undercut by someone scrolling the commit log.
handling_the_scaffolding_question.guidance: Do not volunteer the tool's brand name; do not deny the approach if asked directly.

evidence_level_legend.VERIFIED: Directly supported by code, production data, git history or documentation
evidence_level_legend.DERIVED: Calculated from verified evidence; calculation shown
evidence_level_legend.STRONGLY_SUPPORTED: Multiple pieces of evidence point the same way but it cannot be proven outright
evidence_level_legend.INFERRED: Likely from architecture or context; direct evidence unavailable
evidence_level_legend.REPORTED: Stated to Abraham by a colleague (here, the CTO) or by Abraham first-hand, verbally and without documentation. Usable with attribution; never as a measured figure.
evidence_level_legend.UNKNOWN: Cannot responsibly be established from available evidence
